newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl, Chirac seek unison amid German-French rift.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, Chirac seek unison amid German-French rift.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl and President Jacques Chirac will be out to stress the positive on Wednesday evening when they meet in Bonn for informal talks amid growing signs of Franco-German differences over Europe.

Bonn diplomats and officials say the two, whose countries form the core alliance pushing forward European integration, would probably discuss Europe's single currency, EU reform plans and possibly NATO's eastward expansion over dinner.
They said Kohl and Chirac would probably not reveal much about their talks since their only meeting with the press is scheduled for 1730 GMT, before the dinner gets under way.
"This is part of the regular series of meetings they have every six to eight weeks," one official said.

International markets will be looking for any statement about the euro currency as pressure mounts on Bonn to square its dogged insistence on strict compliance with the Maastricht criteria with growing signs that Germany will not meet them.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel denied reports on Monday that he had relaxed efforts to match Bonn's budget deficit to the three percent of gross domestic product target laid out for entry into economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

Serious differences over Europe's future emerged at an EU foreign ministers' meeting in Noordwijk over the weekend when France pushed hard for a radical reduction in the number of European commissioners each member state can have.
Stressing the commission would become unwieldy if it expanded each time new members joined the EU, Paris proposed reducing the 20-member body to 10-12 rotating seats.
Consensus-minded Germany, aware of the stiff opposition to this from smaller EU members, leans towards a compromise that would allow all members to have a seat.
"The French proposal cannot be achieved for political reasons," said one foreign policy strategist in Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

"The fact there are now so many proposals for rotation, junior commissioners without portfolio and so on only shows we are still at the start of this debate," he said. "It will probably not be solved until the Amsterdam summit in June."
Linked to this issue is the question of the weighting of member's votes within the Council of Ministers to reflect the size of their respective populations.

Each enlargement of the EU undermines the dominant role the largest states -- Germany, France, Britain and Italy -- used to play by increasing the number of votes the smaller countries can amass against them.
The issue was hardly discussed at Noordwijk because the ministers were distracted by a dispute over whether to condemn China over its human rights record.
Although it seems like a case of squaring a circle, German officials insist Bonn and Paris will be able to come up with some sort of compromise in time for the Amsterdam summit.
Taking a longer view, the two countries' foreign ministries are considering ways to improve their own policy coordination to present a more united front in foreign affairs.
They have worked out proposals for closer consultation on the main issues, joint trips abroad by their foreign ministers and more personnel swaps between German and French ministries.
The suggestions are still at the planning stage and will not be on the agenda for Kohl and Chirac, a spokesman said.
German press commentators were not as optimistic as Bonn about the chances of effective reforms coming in Amsterdam.

"The loudly proclaimed project of updating the Maastricht treaty is bogged down in crisis," Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung wrote on Wednesday. "Apart from calls to hang on, there is nothing that points to any success of these talks soon."
